title: If We Are Setting Assessments That a Robot Can Complete, What Does That Say About Our Assessments? -what-does-that-say-about-our-assessments-cbc1871f502
author: Christodoulou, Daisy
summary: Daisy Christodoulou rebuts the popular post-ChatGPT argument, voiced by figures from Dan Fitzpatrick to Marc Andreessen to Daniel Susskind, that if a computer can complete a school assessment, the assessment itself must be inadequate and needs to be made harder or more "human." She identifies three flawed assumptions behind that claim. First, invoking Moravec's paradox, she notes computers have always found the routine academic skills schools test comparatively easy, while genuinely human skills like perception and mobility are the hard problems for AI, so "set assessments computers can't do" was never really achievable. Second, she argues advanced skills cannot be reached by leapfrogging fundamental ones, since working memory limits mean students need automatic, long-term-memory-stored basics before they can do the higher-order thinking everyone wants, using a chess analogy to make the point concrete. Third, she distinguishes the "sample" (the test itself) from the "domain" (the student's actual understanding), arguing via Daniel Koretz that a test score only matters insofar as it reflects the domain, so a computer besting a student's essay says nothing about whether the assessment was worthwhile, because the value was always in the student's own process, not the output's competitiveness with a machine.
points: Christodoulou's use of Moravec's paradox reframes the entire premise of the "robot-proof assessment" argument: computers have always found typical school-taught skills easy, so the goalpost was never reachable in the way critics imply.

Her working-memory argument supplies the mechanism for why fundamentals can't be skipped: information has to be stored in long-term memory to be "effortlessly and frictionlessly summoned" alongside environmental information, which is what produces skill.

The sample-versus-domain distinction, credited to Daniel Koretz, is her sharpest reframe: a test's value depends entirely on what it tells you about a student's broader understanding, not on whether a machine could also pass it.

She flags a motivational risk specific to the AI moment: students who spend an hour struggling with an essay only to see ChatGPT outperform them in seconds may become demotivated unless teachers explicitly reframe what the task was actually for.
quotes: The basic technological principle here is Moravec’s paradox, first developed in 1988, which is that computers find the types of academic skills we teach and assess in schools trivially easy.

In order for students to successfully grapple with problems computers cannot do, they must work through problems that computers can do. If schools could only teach maths using problems that computers cannot solve, we would have to teach six-year-olds maths using problems even top mathematicians find difficult!

Thinking well requires knowing facts, and that’s true not simply because you need something to think about. The very processes that teachers care about most — critical thinking processes such as reasoning and problem solving — are intimately intertwined with factual knowledge that is stored in long-term memory.

Test scores reflect a small sample of behaviour and are valuable only insofar as they support conclusions about the larger domains of interest. This is perhaps the most fundamental principle of achievement testing.
If a student struggles for an hour over an extended piece of writing and then finds that a computer has surpassed it in seconds, it is entirely possible they will feel demotivated.
